desc:
Numbers arrive one at a time in the order of nums. After each arrival, report the p-th percentile of everything received so far, using the nearest-rank rule: if m numbers have arrived, take the sorted numbers and report the one at 1-based rank ceil(p * m / 100).

With p = 50 this is the lower median; with p = 100 it is the maximum so far.

nums = [7, 3, 9, 1, 5, 8], p = 75
m=1: rank 1 of [7]               -> 7
m=2: rank 2 of [3,7]             -> 7
m=3: rank 3 of [3,7,9]           -> 9
m=4: rank 3 of [1,3,7,9]         -> 7
m=5: rank 4 of [1,3,5,7,9]       -> 7
m=6: rank 5 of [1,3,5,7,8,9]     -> 8
answer = [7, 7, 9, 7, 7, 8]
hints: The answer is the element of rank r in the sorted prefix, where r = ceil(p * m / 100) changes by at most one when a number arrives.
Generalise the median trick: keep the r smallest numbers in a max-heap and all the others in a min-heap. The percentile is the root of the max-heap.
On each arrival, push the number into the correct heap, then move roots across until the max-heap has exactly r elements for the new m.
editorial: The median structure is the special case where the lower heap holds the first half. Here the lower max-heap lo must hold exactly the r = ceil(p * m / 100) smallest numbers, and then its root is precisely the rank-r element. The upper min-heap hi holds the rest.

When a number x arrives (so m grows by one), put it into lo if it is at most the root of lo, otherwise into hi; this keeps the order between the heaps. Then compute the new r. Because r grows by at most one per arrival, but the insertion may have gone to the wrong side by one, a loop that moves roots from lo to hi while lo is too big, and from hi to lo while it is too small, runs at most a couple of iterations.
Integer arithmetic for the rank: (p * m + 99) // 100 is ceil(p * m / 100). Since p ≥ 1 the rank is at least 1, so lo is never empty. Overall O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
